name: Apache TinkerPop (Gremlin)
summary: An open-source graph computing framework and its traversal language, Gremlin: one API and one language that run on more than two dozen graph databases, and on Spark for analytics.
intro: TinkerPop is a set of interfaces plus the software around them. Graph providers implement the Structure API, which describes vertices, edges and properties; users write traversals against the Process API. Gremlin is the traversal language: a functional, data-flow chain of steps such as `V()`, `has()`, `out()` and `values()`, run by the Gremlin traversal machine. Because the language is separate from the machine, other query languages can be compiled to run on TinkerPop systems. Gremlin is embedded in host languages, with official variants for Java, Groovy, Python, .NET, JavaScript and Go, so a traversal is ordinary code rather than a query string. Gremlin Server exposes a graph as a network endpoint on port 8182 that these clients send traversals to, and TinkerGraph is the in-memory reference database. The same traversal can run as a real-time OLTP query or as an OLAP job through `GraphComputer`, which processes the graph in parallel, for example on Spark.

Systems that implement TinkerPop include JanusGraph, Amazon Neptune, Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin, DataStax DSE Graph, Aerospike Graph, ArcadeDB, HugeGraph, ArangoDB and PuppyGraph. TinkerPop does no storage of its own: indexing, transactions and scaling come from whichever provider runs it. The current line is 3.8 (3.8.2 was released on 1 September 2026; 3.8.0 in November 2025 added a `gremlin-mcp` server for AI agents). TinkerPop 4 is in beta: 4.0.0-beta.3 in July 2026 continued the move from WebSockets to HTTP, rewrote the `match()` step to accept declarative subqueries with a subset of GQL as the reference, and made multi-label vertices optional.
strengths: Portable: one language and driver family across many databases and clouds, including Neptune, Cosmos DB and JanusGraph
The same traversal runs as a quick OLTP query or as a parallel OLAP job on Spark
Traversals are written in the host language (Java, Python, JavaScript, .NET, Go), not assembled as strings
Run by the Apache Software Foundation under Apache 2.0, with TinkerGraph and Gremlin Server for local development
limits: Step-by-step traversals are harder to read than pattern-matching languages like Cypher for many questions, and the 2024 ISO standard for property graphs is GQL, not Gremlin
A framework, not a database: performance, indexes, transactions and the exact set of supported steps depend on the provider

TinkerPop 4 brings breaking changes (HTTP instead of WebSockets, a new transaction API, removal of bytecode in favour of string-based traversals) and was still in beta in October 2026, well after its roadmap’s 2025 target

story: TinkerPop started in 2009 at the Los Alamos National Laboratory as a group of open-source graph tools. TinkerPop1, released in 2011, was a toolkit called Blueprints, Pipes, Frames, Furnace and Rexster, with Gremlin as its traversal language; TinkerPop2 followed in 2012.

TinkerPop3 brought those pieces into one framework centred on Gremlin, a graph traversal machine and language, with the same traversals running against transactional databases and batch processors. The project entered the Apache Incubator in January 2015 and became a top-level project on 23 May 2016, when it shipped reference implementations for Neo4j (OLTP) and for Giraph, Spark and Hadoop (OLAP) and was in use at DataStax, IBM and Amazon, which ran its order-fulfilment graph of about a trillion edges on it.

Graph databases and cloud services adopted Gremlin as a common interface, including Amazon Neptune and Azure Cosmos DB. Since ISO published GQL in 2024, TinkerPop 4 has worked toward HTTP transport, string-based traversals and a `match()` step that accepts declarative languages, with a GQL subset as its reference.

choices.choice: A standard API instead of a database
choices.why: Graph vendors could implement one set of interfaces, and users would get the same language, server and tools on any of them.

choices.choice: The language separate from the machine
choices.why: Gremlin traversals compile to steps run by the Gremlin machine, so other languages, such as SPARQL or SQL, can be compiled to run on the same systems.

choices.choice: OLTP and OLAP from one traversal
choices.why: The same Gremlin can answer a small neighbourhood query in real time or run across a cluster with `GraphComputer`, from one machine to graphs with billions of edges.
Writing Gremlin as Java, Python or JavaScript code lets developers use their own language and tooling instead of building query strings.
